prompt.context: You are a consultant advising a construction company. The major line of business for your client is road construction. They have recently entered into building construction. In the past they have grown through acquisitions.
prompt.question: The COO has hired you to help them increase ROA. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: How does our ROA compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors have better ROA than us. When we started it was good but then it has been going continuously down.

clarifying_info.q: What are the profit margins and how do they compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Our profit margins have been almost equivalent to those of competitors.

clarifying_info.q: Have revenues gone up or down recently?
clarifying_info.a: We have not seen any drop in revenues; it has been growing with the market.

clarifying_info.q: How does our COGS as a percentage of revenue compare?
clarifying_info.a: We are not much off but there may be some opportunities on the cost side.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major labor and raw material costs?
clarifying_info.a: Labor costs are competitive. Major raw materials are concrete, crushed stone, and steel.

framework: Break ROA into its two drivers: Income (numerator) and Assets (denominator)
Income side: analyze revenue trends, profit margins vs. competitors, and cost structure (labor, raw materials)
Asset side: identify unutilized or redundant assets on the balance sheet, especially from acquisitions
Growth side: evaluate new business lines (building construction) for revenue and margin opportunity
Cost reduction: explore vertical integration for key raw material inputs

questions.prompt: What is driving the decline in ROA — is it an income problem or an asset problem?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that profit margins are roughly in line with competitors and revenues are growing, so the primary culprit is the asset base, not the income statement. The company has grown through acquisitions and accumulated underutilized buildings, offices, and equipment that sit on the balance sheet without generating returns.

questions.prompt: What can be done on the asset side to improve ROA?
questions.guidance: Key insight: sell unutilized assets acquired through past acquisitions. These assets are not generating income but inflate the denominator of ROA, dragging the ratio down. Identifying this is the core of the case — the interviewer notes that focusing only on the income statement is 25% of the answer.

questions.prompt: What revenue growth opportunity exists beyond road construction?
questions.guidance: The client recently entered building construction. A strong candidate probes this new business line: How is it performing? What are the margins? The answer is that building construction carries a high profit margin. Increasing business in this segment is a lever to grow income and improve ROA.

questions.prompt: What cost reduction opportunity exists on the raw material side?
questions.guidance: Crushed stone is a major raw material input. Vertical integration — acquiring or partnering with stone crushers — would reduce raw material costs and improve profit margins, further lifting ROA.

recommendation: Divest unutilized assets (buildings, offices, equipment) inherited from past acquisitions to reduce the asset base and immediately improve ROA
Expand the building construction business line, which carries higher profit margins, to grow net income
Pursue vertical integration with stone crushers to reduce raw material costs and widen margins
risks: Asset sales may take time to execute and realize cash; market conditions may limit sale prices
Rapid expansion in building construction requires management bandwidth and capital, which may be constrained
Vertical integration in stone crushing requires upfront capital and introduces operational complexity outside the core competency
next_steps: Conduct a full asset audit to identify and quantify all underutilized assets from acquisitions
Assess the building construction pipeline and capacity to scale that business unit
Model the economics of acquiring a stone crusher supplier vs. long-term supply contracts
